analysis.one_liner: Requires federal agencies and polluters to prevent disproportionate pollution harm to communities of color and low-income communities.
analysis.headline: Sponsored by 15 senators in August 2020, the bill was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it easier for people in communities of color, low-income communities, and tribal communities to sue over pollution that hits them hardest, by restoring a civil rights tool that lets them show a policy has a discriminatory effect even if it looks neutral. It would require federal agencies to study the combined pollution burden on a community before approving major projects, tighten permits for big polluters, and deny permits to companies that repeatedly violate the law. It would also require ingredient labels on cosmetics and menstrual products, fund parks and transit to public lands in underserved areas, and help workers and towns that depend on fossil fuels adjust to a cleaner economy.
analysis.who_benefits: Communities of color, low-income neighborhoods, and tribal and indigenous communities living near pollution sources gain new legal standing, tougher permit reviews that consider all the pollution they already breathe and drink, community impact reports before federal projects, and grant money for parks, transit to trails, and community health programs. Consumers gain ingredient disclosure on cosmetics and menstrual products. Workers and towns dependent on fossil fuels gain transition assistance and economic revitalization funding.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Communities near pollution; consumers; fossil-fuel towns

how_it_helps.text: Amends the Civil Rights Act of 1964 so a person can sue a federal agency over a policy that has a discriminatory effect based on race, color, or national origin, even without proving intent, and lets them recover attorney's fees [S2] [S3].

Requires Clean Air Act and Clean Water Act permits for major pollution sources to account for cumulative pollution already affecting a community, with a 'reasonable certainty of no harm' standard, and requires repeat violators to submit compliance plans or face permit denial [S3].

Requires federal agencies preparing environmental reviews for projects affecting environmental justice communities to produce community impact reports, hold 90-day comment periods, provide translations, and consider community-proposed alternatives [S3].

Creates grant programs for community-based groups, urban park access, and a Transit to Trails program connecting underserved communities to parks and public lands, with $10 million per year authorized for transit grants [S3].

Requires ingredient labeling on cosmetics and menstrual products, funds research into safer chemical alternatives, and provides revenues for just-transition assistance and economic revitalization for fossil-fuel-dependent communities [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Fossil fuel plants, refineries, waste facilities, and other major pollution sources would face costlier and slower permitting, mandatory compliance plans for repeat violations, and greater litigation exposure. Cosmetic, personal-care, menstrual-product, and chemical makers would bear labeling and reformulation costs. Federal agencies would bear new reporting, training, and lawsuit obligations.

drawbacks.text: The cumulative-impact permit standard ('reasonable certainty of no harm') would make it harder and slower to issue or renew Clean Air Act and Clean Water Act permits for major sources, and companies and some states argue such tests can stall needed infrastructure and energy projects [S3].

The bill gives any aggrieved person the right to sue federal agencies over Title VI violations and directs attorney's fees to prevailing plaintiffs, which creates litigation exposure and could slow agency programs while cases are decided [S3].

The urban park and transit-to-trails grant programs require a 100 percent match from state, local, or private sources unless waived, a requirement that can screen out exactly the under-resourced communities the programs target [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefits — restoring a civil rights remedy for discriminatory pollution, forcing permit decisions to count the pollution a community already carries, and disclosure of toxic ingredients — are substantial for the people who have historically borne the most pollution. The costs are real but manageable: higher permitting complexity and litigation risk for industry and agencies, and some program design flaws (like the full matching requirement) that could undercut equity goals without fixes.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee the day it was introduced and sat there without a hearing, markup, or vote until the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Kamala Harris introduced the bill on August 3, 2020, joined by 14 cosponsors (13 Democrats and 1 Independent), and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee that same day [S4] [S5].
The action history shows no further steps: no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S5].
Because it died in committee, none of its provisions took effect, including the civil rights amendments, cumulative-impact permit standards, and labeling requirements [S3] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Major polluters and federal agencies are better off because the bill died: they avoid the cumulative-impact permit tests, persistent-violator provisions, private lawsuits, and product labeling mandates. The overburdened communities the bill targeted gained nothing.

for.name: Sen. Kamala Harris
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the Senate on August 3, 2020.

for.name: 14 Senate cosponsors (13 Democrats, 1 Independent)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Sens. Duckworth, Booker, Warren, Feinstein, Wyden, Durbin, Smith, Blumenthal, Markey, Schatz, Merkley, Gillibrand, Udall, and Sanders.

against.name: Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred (chaired by Sen. John Barrasso, R-WY)
against.what_they_did: Took no action after the bill was referred; no hearing, markup, or committee vote was ever scheduled.

against.name: Sen. Mitch McConnell
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor; the bill remained a committee referral for its entire life.

sides.party_line_note: All 15 original sponsors were Democrats or one Independent and no Republican cosponsored; the bill died in a committee and a Senate both controlled by Republicans.

industries.industry: Major pollution sources (fossil fuel plants, refineries, industrial and waste facilities)
industries.note: Permits for major sources would have to analyze cumulative pollution affecting nearby census block groups and meet a 'reasonable certainty of no harm' standard, and persistent violators would face compliance-plan requirements or permit denial. Their interest in the bill ran against communities seeking cleaner air and water.

industries.industry: Chemical and consumer product makers (cosmetics, personal care, menstrual products, cleaning, toy, and baby products)
industries.note: The bill requires ingredient lists and warnings on products like cosmetics and menstrual products and funds research into safer chemical alternatives, adding disclosure and reformulation costs.
The bill funds capacity-building grants for community organizations and gives them, along with residents, standing and attorney's fees to challenge discriminatory agency actions.

industries.industry: State and local park agencies and outdoor recreation
industries.note: Grant programs would fund parkland acquisition, recreation facilities, and transit connections to parks in underserved urban and rural areas, financed partly by redirecting Gulf of Mexico energy revenue-sharing.
